items.text: We introduce RAG models where the parametric memory is a pre-trained seq2seq model and the non-parametric memory is a dense vector index of Wikipedia, accessed with a pre-trained neural retriever.
items.why: Defines core RAG architecture components.
items.plain: We introduce RAG models where the fixed memory is a sequence-to-sequence model and the external memory is a searchable vector index of Wikipedia accessed via a neural retriever.

items.text: We compare two RAG formulations, one which conditions on the same retrieved passages across the whole generated sequence, and another which can use different passages per token.
items.why: Introduces the two core RAG model formulations.
items.plain: We compare two RAG models: one uses the same retrieved text passages for the whole sequence, while the other can use different passages for each word.

items.text: We combine a pre-trained retriever (Query Encoder + Document Index) with a pre-trained seq2seq model (Generator) and ﬁne-tune end-to-end.
items.why: Summarizes the overall system pipeline and training.
items.plain: We combine a neural retriever with a sequence-to-sequence language model and train them together from start to finish.

items.text: For query x, we use Maximum Inner Product Search (MIPS) to ﬁnd the top-K documents zi.
items.why: Explains how documents are retrieved using MIPS.
items.plain: For an input query, we use Maximum Inner Product Search to find the top K most relevant document passages.

items.text: For ﬁnal prediction y, we treat z as a latent variable and marginalize over seq2seq predictions given different documents.
items.why: States how predictions marginalize over retrieved documents.
items.plain: To make the final prediction, we treat the retrieved document as a hidden variable and average predictions across different documents.

items.text: The retriever (Dense Passage Retriever [26], henceforth DPR) provides latent documents conditioned on the input, and the seq2seq model (BART [32]) then conditions on these latent documents together with the input to generate the output.
items.why: Specifies exact model choices for retriever and generator.
items.plain: The retriever (Dense Passage Retriever) finds documents based on the input, and the sequence-to-sequence model (BART) uses those documents and the input to generate text.

items.text: We marginalize the latent documents with a top-K approximation, either on a per-output basis (assuming the same document is responsible for all tokens) or a per-token basis (where different documents are responsible for different tokens).
items.why: Explains document marginalization granularities.
items.plain: We average candidate documents using a top-K approximation, either across the full output sequence or separately for each output token.

items.text: Like T5 [51] or BART, RAG can be ﬁne-tuned on any seq2seq task, whereby both the generator and retriever are jointly learned.
items.why: Notes fine-tuning flexibility and joint learning.
items.plain: RAG can be fine-tuned on any task converting text sequences to other text sequences, training both generator and retriever together.

items.text: As shown in Figure 1, our models leverage two components: (i) a retriever pη(z|x) with parameters η that returns (top-K truncated) distributions over text passages given a query x and (ii) a generator pθ(yi|x, z, y1:i−1) parametrized
items.why: Defines mathematical role of retriever and generator.
items.plain: Our framework uses a retriever that provides a probability distribution over text passages given a query, and a generator that produces output tokens based on prior tokens, the input query, and a retrieved passage.

items.text: To train the retriever and generator end-to-end, we treat the retrieved document as a latent variable.
items.why: States training formulation using latent variables.
items.plain: To train the retriever and generator end-to-end, we treat the retrieved document as an unobserved latent variable.

items.text: In one approach, RAG-Sequence, the model uses the same document to predict each target token.
items.why: Defines the RAG-Sequence model approach.
items.plain: In RAG-Sequence, the model uses the same retrieved document to predict every target token in a generated sequence.

items.text: The second approach, RAG-Token, can predict each target token based on a different document.
items.why: Defines the RAG-Token model approach.
items.plain: In RAG-Token, the model can predict each individual token in the target sequence using a different retrieved document.

items.text: Technically, it treats the retrieved document as a single latent variable that is marginalized to get the seq2seq probability p(y|x) via a top-K approximation.
items.why: Explains RAG-Sequence probability calculation.
items.plain: The model treats the retrieved document as a hidden variable and sums probabilities across the top K retrieved documents to calculate the overall sequence probability.

items.text: RAG-Token Model In the RAG-Token model we can draw a different latent document for each target token and marginalize accordingly.
items.why: Explains RAG-Token probability calculation mechanism.
items.plain: In the RAG-Token model, we can pick a different latent document for each target word and average probabilities at every step.

items.text: This allows the generator to choose content from several documents when producing an answer.
items.why: Explains benefit of RAG-Token approach.
items.plain: This design allows the model to gather information from multiple retrieved documents when producing a single answer.

items.text: Finally, we note that RAG can be used for sequence classiﬁcation tasks by considering the target class as a target sequence of length one, in which case RAG-Sequence and RAG-Token are equivalent.
items.why: Explains RAG setup for classification tasks.
items.plain: RAG can perform sequence classification by treating the output label as a single token, which makes RAG-Sequence and RAG-Token mathematically identical.

items.text: where d(z) is a dense representation of a document produced by a BERTBASE document encoder [8], and q(x) a query representation produced by a query encoder, also based on BERTBASE.
items.why: Defines vector representations in DPR retriever.
items.plain: The retriever computes a dense vector for documents using a BERT document encoder and a query vector using a BERT query encoder.

items.text: Calculating top-k(pη(·|x)), the list of k documents z with highest prior probability pη(z|x), is a Maximum Inner Product Search (MIPS) problem, which can be approximately solved in sub-linear time [23].
items.why: Describes efficient sub-linear time document retrieval.
items.plain: Finding the top K documents with the highest prior probability is a Maximum Inner Product Search problem solved in sub-linear time.

items.text: We use a pre-trained bi-encoder from DPR to initialize our retriever and to build the document index.
items.why: States initialization details for retriever component.
items.plain: We initialize our retriever and build our document index using a pre-trained dual-encoder from Dense Passage Retriever.

items.text: We use BART-large [32], a pre-trained seq2seq transformer [58] with 400M parameters.
items.why: Specifies exact generator model size and architecture.
items.plain: We use BART-large, a pre-trained sequence-to-sequence transformer with 400 million parameters, as our generator.

items.text: To combine the input x with the retrieved content z when generating from BART, we simply concatenate them.
items.why: Describes simple input string combination mechanism.
items.plain: To combine the input text with the retrieved document for BART, we concatenate them together.

items.text: We jointly train the retriever and generator components without any direct supervision on what document should be retrieved.
items.why: States key unsupervised retrieval training assumption.
items.plain: We train the retriever and generator together without explicit labels specifying which document should be retrieved.

items.text: minimize the negative marginal log-likelihood of each target, P
items.why: Defines training loss function objective.
items.plain: We minimize the negative marginal log-likelihood of each target output.

items.text: We do not ﬁnd this step necessary for strong performance, and keep the document encoder (and index) ﬁxed, only ﬁne-tuning the query encoder BERTq and the BART generator.
items.why: Explains parameters fine-tuned versus kept frozen.
items.plain: We keep the document encoder and document index fixed during training, fine-tuning only the query encoder and the BART generator.

items.text: z∈top-k(p(·|x)) pη(zi|x)pθ(yi|x, zi, y1:i−1) To decode, we can plug p′
items.why: Describes decoding process for RAG-Token.
items.plain: RAG-Token acts as a standard autoregressive generator whose step probability sums over the top K retrieved documents, enabling decoding via standard beam search.

items.text: Instead, we run beam search for each document z, scoring each hypothesis using pθ(yi|x, z, y1:i−1).
items.why: Explains document-level beam search in RAG-Sequence.
items.plain: For RAG-Sequence, we run a separate beam search for each document and score the candidates using the generator model.

items.text: To estimate the probability of an hypothesis y we run an additional forward pass for each document z for which y does not appear in the beam, multiply generator probability with pη(z|x) and then sum the probabilities across beams for the marginals.
items.why: Details thorough decoding marginalization in RAG-Sequence.
items.plain: To evaluate a candidate output sequence, we run extra forward passes for documents where it did not appear in the beam, multiply by document retrieval probabilities, and sum across documents.

items.text: For more efﬁcient decoding, we can make a further approximation that pθ(y|x, zi) ≈0 where y was not generated during beam search from x, zi.
items.why: Defines fast decoding approximation for RAG-Sequence.
items.plain: For faster decoding, we assume generator probability is zero for sequences not generated during beam search for a given document.

items.text: Each Wikipedia article is split into disjoint 100-word chunks, to make a total of 21M documents.
items.why: Details Wikipedia document chunking experimental setup.
items.plain: Each Wikipedia article is split into non-overlapping 100-word chunks, creating 21 million documents total.

items.text: We use the document encoder to compute an embedding for each document, and build a single MIPS index using FAISS [23] with a Hierarchical Navigable Small World approximation for fast retrieval [37].
items.why: Describes index creation with FAISS framework.
items.plain: We encode each document into a vector and build a single vector search index using FAISS with a Hierarchical Navigable Small World approximation.

items.text: We consider k ∈{5, 10} for training and set k for test time using dev data.
items.why: Specifies top-k hyperparameter settings for experiments.
items.plain: We train with 5 or 10 retrieved documents and select the best number of retrieved documents for testing using validation data.

items.text: We treat questions and answers as input-output text pairs (x, y) and train RAG by directly minimizing the negative log-likelihood of answers.
items.why: Describes open-domain QA training methodology.
items.plain: We treat questions and answers as text pairs and train RAG by directly minimizing the answer's negative log-likelihood.

items.text: As CT and WQ are small, we follow DPR [26] by initializing CT and WQ models with our NQ RAG model.
items.why: States initialization strategy for small QA datasets.
items.plain: Because CuratedTrec and WebQuestions are small datasets, we initialize their models using our Natural Questions RAG model.

items.text: We do not use the supplied passages, only the questions and answers, to treat
items.why: Clarifies open-domain evaluation on MS MARCO.
items.plain: We discard the provided search passages and use only questions and answers to evaluate MS MARCO as an open-domain generation task.

items.text: We map FEVER class labels (supports, refutes, or not enough info) to single output tokens and directly train with claim-class pairs.
items.why: Explains adaptation of RAG for classification.
items.plain: We map target labels to single output tokens and train directly on claim-class pairs.

items.text: Crucially, unlike most other approaches to FEVER, we do not use supervision on retrieved evidence.
items.why: Highlights absence of explicit retrieval supervision.
items.plain: Unlike most other methods on FEVER, we do not train using supervised annotations for retrieved evidence.

items.text: On all four open-domain QA tasks, RAG sets a new state of the art (only on the T5-comparable split for TQA).
items.why: Summarizes main SOTA result on open QA.
items.plain: RAG sets a new state-of-the-art score across all four open-domain question answering benchmarks.

items.text: Unlike REALM and T5+SSM, RAG enjoys strong results without expensive, specialized “salient span masking” pre-training [20].
items.why: Compares training efficiency against rival architectures.
items.plain: RAG achieves strong results without requiring expensive, specialized pre-training objectives like salient span masking.

items.text: RAG demonstrates that neither a re-ranker nor extractive reader is necessary for state-of-the-art performance.
items.why: Shows state-of-the-art results without re-rankers.
items.plain: RAG demonstrates that state-of-the-art performance does not require a re-ranking model or an extractive reading model.

items.text: Furthermore, RAG can generate correct answers even when the correct answer is not in any retrieved document, achieving 11.8% accuracy in such cases for NQ, where an extractive model would score 0%.
items.why: Provides evidence on generating non-retrieved correct answers.
items.plain: RAG achieves 11.8% accuracy on Natural Questions even when the correct answer is missing from all retrieved documents, whereas extractive models score 0%.

items.text: As shown in Table 2, RAG-Sequence outperforms BART on Open MS-MARCO NLG by 2.6 Bleu points and 2.6 Rouge-L points.
items.why: Reports empirical performance on abstractive QA.
items.plain: RAG-Sequence outperforms BART on Open MS-MARCO NLG by 2.6 BLEU points and 2.6 ROUGE-L points.

items.text: Table 2 shows that RAG-Token performs better than RAG-Sequence on Jeopardy question generation, with both models outperforming BART on Q-BLEU-1.
items.why: Reports comparative performance on Jeopardy generation.
items.plain: RAG-Token scores higher than RAG-Sequence on Jeopardy question generation, and both outperform BART on Q-BLEU-1.

items.text: Evaluators indicated that BART was more factual than RAG in only 7.1% of cases, while RAG was more factual in 42.7% of cases, and both RAG and BART were factual in a further 17% of cases, clearly demonstrating the effectiveness of RAG on the task over a state-of-the-art generation model.
items.why: Provides human evaluation evidence for factuality gains.
items.plain: Human evaluators found BART more factual in only 7.1% of cases, compared to 42.7% for RAG.

items.text: Jeopardy questions often contain two separate pieces of information, and RAG-Token may perform best because it can generate responses that combine content from several documents.
items.why: Provides intuition for why RAG-Token succeeds.
items.plain: RAG-Token may work best on Jeopardy questions because it can synthesize information combined from multiple retrieved documents.

items.text: This example shows how parametric and non-parametric memories work together—the non-parametric component helps to guide the generation, drawing out speciﬁc knowledge stored in the parametric memory.
items.why: Explains synergy between parametric and non-parametric memory.
items.plain: The retrieved external text helps direct generation while retrieving specific factual information already stored in the model's internal parameters.

items.text: For 3-way classiﬁcation, RAG scores are within 4.3% of state-of-the-art models, which are complex pipeline systems with domain-speciﬁc architectures and substantial engineering, trained using intermediate retrieval supervision, which RAG does not require.
items.why: Reports results on FEVER fact verification.
items.plain: For 3-way classification on FEVER, RAG performance comes within 4.3% of specialized pipeline models without using evidence supervision.

items.text: We ﬁnd that the top retrieved document is from a gold article in 71% of cases, and a gold article is present in the top 10 retrieved articles in 90% of cases.
items.why: Quantifies retrieval accuracy on FEVER dataset.
items.plain: The top retrieved document matches gold evidence in 71% of cases, and a gold article appears in the top 10 retrieved articles in 90% of cases.

items.text: Table 5 shows that RAG-Sequence’s generations are more diverse than RAG-Token’s, and both are signiﬁcantly more diverse than BART without needing any diversity-promoting decoding.
items.why: Reports diversity metric improvements over BART baseline.
items.plain: RAG-Sequence generates more diverse text than RAG-Token, and both models generate significantly more diverse text than BART without special decoding strategies.

items.text: As shown in Table 6, learned retrieval improves results for all tasks.
items.why: Shows experimental evidence for joint retriever learning.
items.plain: Learning the retriever during training improves overall performance on all tasks compared to freezing it.

items.text: Differentiable retrieval improves results on all other tasks, especially for Open-Domain QA, where it is crucial.
items.why: Compares dense retrieval performance against BM25 baseline.
items.plain: Differentiable neural retrieval outperforms BM25 on almost all tasks, with the biggest improvement seen in open-domain question answering.

items.text: RAG answers 70% correctly using the 2016 index for 2016 world leaders and 68% using the 2018 index for 2018 world leaders.
items.why: Demonstrates knowledge updates via index hot-swapping.
items.plain: RAG achieves 70% accuracy on 2016 world leaders using a 2016 Wikipedia index, and 68% accuracy on 2018 leaders when swapped to a 2018 index.

items.text: Accuracy with mismatched indices is low (12% with the 2018 index and 2016 leaders, 4% with the 2016 index and 2018 leaders).
items.why: Shows low accuracy when memory index is mismatched.
items.plain: Accuracy drops to 12% or lower when querying world leaders using an index from a non-matching year.

items.text: Effect of Retrieving more documents Models are trained with either 5 or 10 retrieved latent documents, and we do not observe signiﬁcant differences in performance between them.
items.why: Notes effect of retrieved document count in training.
items.plain: Training models with 5 versus 10 retrieved latent documents does not produce significant performance differences.

items.text: Figure 3 (left) shows that retrieving more documents at test time monotonically improves Open-domain QA results for RAG-Sequence, but performance peaks for RAG-Token at 10 retrieved documents.
items.why: Analyzes test-time document count impact on QA.
items.plain: Retrieving more documents at test time consistently improves QA results for RAG-Sequence, whereas RAG-Token performance peaks at 10 documents.

items.text: A key feature of our memory is that it is comprised of raw text rather distributed representations, which makes the memory both (i) human-readable, lending a form of interpretability to our model, and (ii) human-writable, enabling us to dynamically update the model’s memory by editing the document index.
items.why: Highlights advantages of text-based non-parametric memory.
items.plain: Using plain text as memory makes the index readable to humans for interpretability and editable so knowledge can be updated dynamically.

items.text: For Open-domain QA we report test numbers using 15 retrieved documents for RAG-Token models.
items.why: Explains setup for Open-domain QA evaluation using 15 documents.
items.plain: For Open-domain Question Answering, test results use 15 retrieved documents for RAG-Token models.

items.text: For RAG-Sequence models, we report test results using 50 retrieved documents, and we use the Thorough Decoding approach since answers are generally short.
items.why: Details RAG-Sequence document counts and decoding strategy for QA.
items.plain: For RAG-Sequence models, test results use 50 retrieved documents and a Thorough Decoding method because answers are usually short.

items.text: We use greedy decoding for QA as we did not ﬁnd beam search improved results.
items.why: States the decoding choice for Question Answering tasks.
items.plain: Greedy decoding is used for Question Answering because search methods like beam search did not improve performance.

items.text: For Open-MSMarco and Jeopardy question generation, we report test numbers using ten retrieved documents for both RAG-Token and RAG-Sequence, and we also train a BART-large model as a baseline.
items.why: Details retrieval count and baseline for question generation tasks.
items.plain: For Open-MSMarco and Jeopardy question generation, test results use ten retrieved documents for both model types, and a standard large language model named BART-large serves as a baseline.

items.text: We use a beam size of four, and use the Fast Decoding approach for RAG-Sequence models, as Thorough Decoding did not improve performance.
items.why: Describes decoding setup for RAG-Sequence on generation tasks.
items.plain: A beam size of four is used alongside Fast Decoding for RAG-Sequence models, as Thorough Decoding did not improve results.

items.text: We train all RAG models and BART baselines using Fairseq [45].2 We train with mixed precision ﬂoating point arithmetic [40], distributing training across 8, 32GB NVIDIA V100 GPUs, though training and inference can be run on one GPU.
items.why: Describes computational training environment and precision setup.
items.plain: All retrieval-augmented models and baseline models are trained using Fairseq with mixed-precision calculations across eight 32-gigabyte GPUs, though they can run on a single GPU.

items.text: We ﬁnd that doing Maximum Inner Product Search with FAISS is sufﬁciently fast on CPU, so we store document index vectors on CPU, requiring ∼100 GB of CPU memory for all of Wikipedia.
items.why: Details retrieval index memory requirements and hardware placement.
items.plain: Storing document index vectors on a CPU is fast enough using FAISS, requiring about 100 gigabytes of CPU memory for all of Wikipedia.

items.text: For RAG, we also make use of multiple annotation examples for Natural Questions and WebQuestions by training the model with each (q, a) pair separately, leading to a small increase in accuracy.
items.why: Explains training adaptation for datasets with multiple target answers.
items.plain: For Natural Questions and WebQuestions, training the model separately on each question-answer pair slightly improves accuracy.

items.text: For TriviaQA, we ﬁlter out answer candidates if they do not occur in top 1000 documents for the query.
items.why: Explains answer filtering methodology for TriviaQA dataset.
items.plain: For TriviaQA, candidate answers are filtered out if they do not appear in the top 1000 retrieved documents for the prompt.

items.text: For FEVER classiﬁcation, we follow the practice from [32], and ﬁrst re-generate the claim, and then classify using the representation of the ﬁnal hidden state, before ﬁnally marginalizing across documents to obtain the class probabilities.
items.why: Details classification procedure for the FEVER claim verification task.
items.plain: For FEVER classification, the claim is re-generated, categorized using its final hidden state representation, and averaged across documents to calculate class probabilities.

items.text: Our RAG models contain the trainable parameters for the BERT-base query and document encoder of DPR, with 110M parameters each (although we do not train the document encoder ourselves) and 406M trainable parameters from BART-large, 406M parameters, making a total of 626M trainable
items.why: Provides exact parameter breakdown of model components.
items.plain: The model uses 110 million parameters each for a query encoder and a document encoder, plus 406 million parameters from a BART generator, totaling 626 million trainable parameters.

items.text: The T5 model with the closest number of parameters to our models is T5-large (770M parameters), which achieves a score of 28.9 EM on Natural Questions [52], substantially below the 44.5 that RAG-Sequence achieves, indicating that hybrid parametric/nonparametric models require far fewer trainable parameters for strong open-domain QA performance.
items.why: Compares parameter efficiency and performance against a baseline model.
items.plain: A T5-large model with 770 million parameters scores 28.9 exact match on Natural Questions, whereas RAG-Sequence scores 44.5, showing that retrieval models achieve higher accuracy with fewer parameters.

items.text: The non-parametric memory index does not consist of trainable parameters, but does consists of 21M 728 dimensional vectors, consisting of 15.3B values.
items.why: Details structure and storage requirements of non-parametric memory.
items.plain: The non-parametric index consists of 21 million 728-dimensional vectors totaling 15.3 billion values, which can be stored in 8-bit precision.

items.text: In preliminary experiments, we observed that for some tasks such as story generation [11], the retrieval component would “collapse” and learn to retrieve the same documents regardless of the input.
items.why: Describes retrieval collapse failure mode observed on non-factual tasks.
items.plain: In tasks like story generation, the retrieval system collapsed and retrieved identical documents regardless of the prompt.

items.text: In these cases, once retrieval had collapsed, the generator would learn to ignore the documents, and the RAG model would perform equivalently to BART.
items.why: Explains model behavior and degraded performance after retrieval collapse.
items.plain: Once retrieval collapsed, the generator learned to ignore retrieved documents and performed identically to a standard BART model.
